metadata.file_name: 20. Bezek-Güre et al. (2020) Analysis of Factors Effecting PISA 2015 Mathematics Literacy via Educational Data Mining EN.pdf
metadata.title: Analysis of Factors Effecting PISA 2015 Mathematics Literacy via Educational Data Mining

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 Turkey microdata for 15-year-old students, with an analytic sample of 4,422 students drawn from 187 randomly selected schools across 61 provinces. The manuscript describes downloading the PISA dataset and then converting it to Excel, importing into SPSS, and performing data clearance and descriptive statistics before training ML models. It does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the ML training or evaluation steps. Because the paper trains Random Forest and Multi-layer Perceptron models using Weka/SPSS Modeler/Matlab, it is unclear whether complex survey design corrections were incorporated; the safest interpretation is that weights were not explicitly used or not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is constructed from PISA mathematics plausible values by averaging PV1MATH–PV10MATH and then binning into low/medium/high categories. However, the paper does not describe any missing-data strategy for either questionnaire predictors or the PV-derived outcome (e.g., complete-case selection, imputation, or PV-specific handling). Given that PISA datasets typically contain missingness in background variables, this omission is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may affect model generalizability.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2015 Turkey computer-based assessment data. Sampling followed PISA’s design: 187 schools were randomly selected among 61 provinces, and 5,895 students were initially selected; the analytic dataset used for modeling contains 4,422 students (2165 boys and 2257 girls). The manuscript does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules beyond using the available PISA Turkey dataset and performing data clearance in SPSS.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Turkey (15-year-olds) Mathematics literacy (PV1MATH–PV10MATH averaged; binned to low/medium/high)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — Correct classification: 81.2%, Misclassification: 18.8%; Correlation: 0.676193; RMSE: 0.3217; MAE: 0.2064; RAE: 0.5756; RRSE: 0.7377
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Turkey mathematics literacy the study leveraged student anxiety, Turkish language success, mother education level, student motivation, and epistemological beliefs to predict students’ math achievement status (low/medium/high), finding that Random Forest achieved 81.2% correct classification and outperformed the Multi-layer Perceptron on several error metrics. This indicates that strengthening student affective factors (especially anxiety) alongside reading-related achievement and family educational resources may improve mathematics proficiency, though the study is predictive and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 Turkey data for 15-year-old students (analytic sample N=4,422) to predict students’ mathematics literacy proficiency category (low/medium/high). The dependent variable is constructed by averaging PV1MATH–PV10MATH and then applying PISA 2015 proficiency thresholds to create a three-level categorical outcome. Two educational data mining models are compared: a Multi-layer Perceptron neural network and Random Forest, trained using 25 predictors drawn from student questionnaires and background/context variables. Random Forest achieved 81.2% correct classification with correlation 0.676 and lower error metrics (RMSE 0.3217, MAE 0.2064, RRSE 0.7377) than the MLPANN (86.7% correct classification but higher RMSE 0.3927 and RRSE 0.9005). The paper does not report a missing-data strategy and does not document whether PISA sampling/replicate weights were applied, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
